nameStory: The "wormseed" part of this plant's name comes from its historical use as a folk remedy for intestinal worms, though we definitely don't recommend trying this at home! The "wallflower" name refers to its habit of growing in disturbed places like old walls, roadsides, and waste areas - just like someone hanging back at a dance.
description: Wormseed wallflower is a slender annual plant that typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat scraggly appearance. It belongs to the mustard family, which means it has the characteristic four-petaled flowers arranged in a cross shape. The plant produces small, bright yellow flowers clustered at the tips of branching stems, followed by long, thin seed pods. Despite being originally from Europe and Asia, it has naturalized in parts of New England where it grows as a weedy pioneer species.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern, each flower only about 1/4 inch across, clustered at branch tips in elongated groups

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch, arranged alternately up the stem with smooth or slightly toothed edges

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, slender seed pods (siliques) that stick out at angles from the stem, eventually splitting open to release small seeds

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, branching annual that can look somewhat weedy or scraggly, often growing in patches in disturbed soil

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Slender, slightly hairy stems that branch near the top, often with a somewhat angular or ridged texture when you run your fingers along them

habitat: Look for wormseed wallflower in disturbed areas like roadsides, old fields, waste ground, and around parking lots or construction sites. It thrives in poor, sandy or gravelly soils and doesn't compete well with established vegetation. You're most likely to spot it in sunny, open areas where the ground has been recently disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge, forming small rosettes of narrow leaves close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Plants bolt upward and begin flowering from June through August, with the characteristic tiny yellow cross-shaped flowers appearing at branch tips.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall while seed pods mature and split open to disperse seeds. Plants begin to die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died back completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking little wildflower is actually a chemical warfare expert - it produces toxic compounds called cardiac glycosides that can affect heart function in animals, plus mustard oils that give it a peppery bite and help defend against hungry insects!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other small yellow mustard family flowers, but the combination of tiny size (flowers less than 1/4 inch), four-petaled cross shape, and long thin seed pods help distinguish it. Remember: "tiny yellow crosses with skinny pods" for wormseed wallflower.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the "wallflower" name fool you into thinking this is related to garden wallflowers - it's much smaller and weedier looking. Also, despite its folk medicine history, all parts of this plant should be considered potentially toxic due to the cardiac glycosides it contains.
compareHints: Unlike its showier relatives like western wallflower which has larger, more colorful blooms, wormseed wallflower has tiny, pale yellow flowers and a much more weedy appearance. It's also annual rather than perennial like many other wallflowers. Among New England mustards, its combination of very small flowers and long thin pods helps set it apart from similar species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Western wallflower differs from its relatives wormseed wallflower and spreading wallflower primarily in its dense, rounded flower clusters and larger, more fragrant blooms.
Spreading wallflower differs from its cousin wormseed wallflower by its more branched, bushy growth habit and longer seed pods, while wormseed wallflower tends to grow more upright with shorter pods.
